title: What Would Happen If the World Stopped Spinning?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore what would happen if the Earth suddenly stopped spinning. They cover the origin of Earth's rotation via conservation of angular momentum, the gradual slowing of the day length, the immediate effects of a sudden stop (everything unattached hurtling east at about a thousand miles an hour), the ocean shifting toward the poles and resulting map, seismic risk from tectonic plates, year-long days and seasons, impacts on farming, changes to gravity, loss of the Coriolis effect (and the toilet-drain myth), and the magnetic field and atmospheric loss to solar wind. A listener mail from Rachel in Portland about how the podcast helped her through a hard first semester of college closes the episode, followed by sign-off plugs.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about drinking moonshine and beer during the show, then Josh begins the topic with the Earth's formation and why it spins.

segments.title: Why Earth spins and is slowing
segments.summary: The hosts explain that Earth's spin dates from its formation from a rotating disk, citing conservation of angular momentum and Newton's first law. They note the day was about twenty-two hours long four million years ago and is slowing, with a projected day of about twenty-six hours in four hundred million years.

segments.title: Effects of a sudden stop
segments.summary: Josh explains that if Earth stopped suddenly, unattached objects would keep moving eastward at about a thousand miles an hour at the equator, causing catastrophic destruction. They discuss why people do not feel Earth's speed, since the rotation is constant, and why centrifugal force does not fling people off.

segments.title: Oceans, maps and super earthquakes
segments.summary: Seismologists suspect a stop would trigger massive earthquakes via tectonic plate movement. The spin bulges the Earth at the equator and pulls oceans toward it, so they would surge toward the poles, leaving a supercontinent at the equator with an ocean at each pole. Chicago would sit near the northern ocean shore.

segments.title: Year-long day and seasons
segments.summary: A stopped Earth would take a year to do what it now does in a day, so one side would be scorching desert and the other a frozen wasteland. The hosts describe four very different seasons and the difficulty of farming, citing Jonathan At-a-berry's article.

segments.title: Gravity and the Coriolis effect
segments.summary: Gravity would change, strongest at the poles rather than the equator, because centrifugal effects would disappear. The Coriolis effect would be lost; the hosts explain it causes curved paths for travel, and debunk the myth that it determines toilet drain direction.

segments.title: Slowing, drying and magnetic field
segments.summary: The hosts list causes of Earth's slowing, including tidal friction, weather, and earthquakes such as the Japan earthquake that slightly shortened the day. They discuss the magnetic field generated by molten iron, its role in shielding against solar wind, and Earth losing about a ton of atmosphere a day, mostly as water vapor.

segments.title: Listener mail from Rachel
segments.summary: Rachel from Portland writes that the podcast helped her through a difficult transition to the University of Portland, including depression and a breakup. Josh and Chuck respond with encouragement about sticking out hard early college years.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts invite listeners to find them on Twitter, Facebook and by email, and point to the website for more on this and other topics.
